title: Ecosocialism That Doesn’t Address Animal Agriculture Isn’t Serious
author: Jon Hochschartner
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Hog_confinement_barn_interior-680x486.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/27/ecosocialism-
that-doesnt-address-animal-agriculture-isnt-serious/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Hog_confinement_barn_interior-680x486.jpg)

Pigs in a confined feeding factory in the Midwest. Photo: EPA.

I was disappointed to learn the Building for Power campaign, put forward by
the Green New Deal Campaign Commission of the Democratic Socialists of
America, doesn’t seem to address the enormous environmental damage caused by
animal agriculture. Building for Power focuses on four areas: energy, transit,
housing, and public spaces. Unfortunately, our food system is a massive
contributor to climate change, and it’s hard to take seriously an ecosocialism
which doesn’t recognize this and plan accordingly.

I should begin by acknowledging the reasons why I suspect greenhouse-gas
emissions associated with animal agriculture aren’t addressed by Building for
Power. The first is any critical discussion of meat and other animal products
is sure to spark a right-wing backlash. The second is that suggestions for
addressing environmental harms caused by animal agriculture are often
individualistic in nature. Of course, just because a discussion represents a
political third rail doesn’t make it any less necessary, and potential
solutions needn’t be so focused on consumer choices, oblivious to the economic
forces which help shape them.

“Conservative estimates by the United Nations Food and Agriculture
Organization say animal agriculture is responsible for 14.5 percent of all
greenhouse gas emissions globally (the industry has lobbied to reduce that
estimate further, and were successful recently to now say about 12 percent),”
Will Potter writes in his excellent 2025 book, Little Red Barns. “Some
estimates put animal agriculture’s contributions higher, at 28 percent to 37
percent. A report by the WorldWatch Institute placed it at a minimum of 51
percent.” The author noted these numbers don’t factor in the carbon
opportunity costs of rewilding land associated with animal agriculture.

There are many ways ecosocialists could plausibly use the levers of government
to encourage a transition to a more environmentally-friendly food system. One
method would be a massive increase in state and federal funding into
alternative-protein research, in the hopes vegan and cultivated options can
achieve price and taste parity with animal-based protein. Consumers frequently
cite these two factors to explain why they don’t adopt alternative options.
For those who aren’t aware, cultivated meat is grown from livestock cells,
without killing. Scientists believe the product, which remains in early stages
of development, will eventually require a fraction of the greenhouse-gas
emissions necessary to produce slaughtered meat.

In professional taste-test panels run by the nonprofit Food Systems
Innovations, no existing plant-based options fully satisfied omnivores’
expectations, though the Impossible Burger came close, according to Good Food
Institute founder Bruce Friedrich in his fantastic 2026 book, Meat. This makes
sense, given Impossible spent years and millions of dollars developing the
product. I see no reason, however, why it can’t be improved upon, with the
help of artificial intelligence and further human research.

A significant problem for the plant-based sector is there is a wide variation
in quality and those products which come closest to meeting omnivores’ desires
are often significantly more expensive than traditional meat. Ecosocialists
could help address this with publicly-funded, open-access research into vegan
meat. The goal, of course, would be to make the taste of Impossible Burgers
the plant-based sector’s floor, as opposed to its ceiling, and improve upon
taste from there. Such research would aim to lower the costs as well.

In contrast to plant-based meat, cultivated meat is identical to incumbent
options at a cellular level. Unfortunately, I’ve yet to try the product, which
has only been sold in a handful of restaurants, but I’ve heard — aside from an
occasional comment saying the texture needs further work — the taste is
indistinguishable from slaughtered meat. The main barriers to cultivated
products appearing in your local grocery store are various technological
hurdles which, for now, render the protein too expensive to mass produce.

Ecosocialists should back the creation of facilities like the Tufts University
Center for Cellular Agriculture at schools across the country. “Our goal is to
do really good research, and propel educational opportunities for students as
the field grows, and the field will grow,” TUCCA’s director, David Kaplan,
said to Tufts Daily. “At the same time we try and build partnerships with
industry to understand where their needs are going forward.” I have no doubt
that, working together, government-backed scientists can overcome the
technological hurdles impeding the mass production of cultivated meat.

TUCCA has been funded with an initial $10-million grant from President Joe
Biden’s Department of Agriculture, supplemented by $2 million from
Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey’s administration. More recently, Senator
Adam Schiff and Representative Julia Brownley introduced a bill that would
allocate more than $500 million toward the research and development of
alternative proteins, including cultivated meat. Surely self-avowed
ecosocialists can offer more robust funding to this effort to usher in an
environmentally-friendly food system than centrist Democrats like Biden,
Healey, Schiff and Brownley.

Animal agriculture is a leading cause of greenhouse-gas emissions.
Ecosocialists refusing to acknowledge this, and making their policy platform
reflect that reality, due to political inconvenience, isn’t so different from
climate denialism. It’s especially egregious given moderate liberals appear
willing to engage with the issue. The Democratic Socialists of America‘s
Building for Power campaign should include animal agriculture as an area of
focus and agitate for a host of government interventions intended to
transition the country toward an agricultural system centered on greater
consumption of plant-based and cultivated proteins.
